title: Data Science
description: Data wrangling, statistics, and exploratory analysis — the layer beneath machine learning.
blurb: Data wrangling, statistics, and exploratory analysis — the layer beneath machine learning.
careerApplications: Cleaning and understanding data correctly is the unglamorous 80% of real ML/AI work — and the step where most project failures actually start.

lessons.title: What data science is
objectives: Describe the data science workflow end to end
Explain how data science workflow changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect data science workflow with data vs decisions and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Data science is the practice of turning raw, messy data into decisions: collect it, clean it, understand it, and communicate what it means — sometimes ending in a machine learning model, often just ending in an answer to a business question.
examples:
# a typical DS workflow:
# raw CSV/database -> clean & structure -> explore & visualize
# -> statistical summary or ML model -> a decision or a report
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to modeling before understanding the data — most real project time is legitimately spent on cleaning and exploration, not model code.
lessons.careerRelevance: Every AI/ML role assumes this workflow as the starting point, even if the job title says 'ML engineer' not 'data scientist.'

lessons.title: Data collection & data quality
objectives: List common data quality problems and why they matter
Explain how missing data changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect missing data with duplicates and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Data rarely arrives clean: missing values, duplicate rows, inconsistent formats (dates, units), and outliers from data-entry mistakes are the norm, not the exception. Data quality issues silently corrupt every downstream step — a statistic or model built on bad data gives a confident, wrong answer, which is worse than no answer.
examples:
# quality red flags to check first:
# df.isnull().sum()      -- missing values per column
# df.duplicated().sum()  -- exact duplicate rows
# df['date'].dtype       -- is it actually a date, or a string?
commonMistakes: Trusting a dataset just because it 'looks complete' in a spreadsheet preview — always explicitly check for nulls, duplicates, and type mismatches before analyzing.
lessons.careerRelevance: Data-quality bugs are the single most common cause of a wrong conclusion in real analyses.

lessons.title: NumPy fundamentals
objectives: Create and operate on NumPy arrays; explain why NumPy is fast
Explain how ndarray changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect ndarray with vectorization and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: NumPy provides the array — a fixed-type, contiguous block of numbers — and vectorized operations that run in fast compiled code instead of slow Python loops. `arr * 2` multiplies every element without you writing a `for` loop; this vectorization is the performance foundation almost all of Python data science sits on top of.
examples:
import numpy as np
arr = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(arr * 2)          # [2 4 6 8] -- no loop needed
print(arr.mean())       # 2.5
print(arr[arr > 2])     # [3 4] -- boolean filtering
commonMistakes: Writing a Python `for` loop over a NumPy array element by element — this throws away the entire speed advantage; use vectorized operations instead.
lessons.careerRelevance: NumPy is the substrate pandas, scikit-learn, and PyTorch are all built on — this is genuinely foundational, not optional.
lessons.explain: NumPy provides the array — a fixed-type, contiguous block of numbers — and vectorized operations that run in fast compiled code instead of slow Python loops. `arr * 2` multiplies every element without you writing a `for` loop; this vectorization is the performance foundation almost all of Python data science sits on top of.

print(arr[arr > 2])     # [3 4] -- boolean filtering

lessons.title: Pandas fundamentals
objectives: Load, select, and filter data with a pandas DataFrame
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: DataFrame merge / join.
Explain how DataFrame changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect DataFrame with filtering and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A DataFrame is a labeled table — rows and named columns — built on top of NumPy, with tools for exactly the messy, real-world data tasks NumPy alone is clumsy for: reading CSVs, filtering rows by condition, grouping and aggregating.
examples:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('sales.csv')
recent = df[df['year'] >= 2024]
by_region = df.groupby('region')['revenue'].sum()
commonMistakes: Modifying a DataFrame slice and being surprised it didn't change the original — pandas' `SettingWithCopyWarning` exists precisely because this is a common, confusing gotcha.
lessons.careerRelevance: Pandas is the day-to-day tool of virtually every data science and ML role that touches tabular data. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Data cleaning
objectives: Handle missing values and inconsistent data systematically
Explain how missing-value strategies changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect missing-value strategies with standardization and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Cleaning means deciding, deliberately, what to do with each quality problem: drop rows with missing values, fill them with a sensible default (mean, median, or a flag value), standardize formats (dates, casing, units), and remove true duplicates.
examples:
df['age'] = df['age'].fillna(df['age'].median())
df['email'] = df['email'].str.lower().str.strip()
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=['user_id'])
commonMistakes: Silently dropping all rows with any missing value — this can throw away a large, non-random chunk of your data and bias every result that follows.
lessons.careerRelevance: Cleaning decisions materially change model/analysis outcomes — being able to justify them is a real interview and code-review topic.

lessons.title: Descriptive statistics
objectives: Compute and interpret mean, median, standard deviation, and quartiles
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: confidence interval intuition, hypothesis testing, A/B testing, correlation vs causation.
Explain how mean vs median changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect mean vs median with standard deviation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Descriptive statistics summarize a dataset in a few numbers: mean and median describe the 'center' (median is robust to outliers, mean isn't), standard deviation describes spread, and quartiles show the distribution's shape.
examples:
df['price'].describe()
# count, mean, std, min, 25%, 50% (median), 75%, max
# a huge gap between mean and median usually signals outliers
commonMistakes: Reporting only the mean when the data is skewed — a single huge outlier can drag the mean far from what a typical row actually looks like; the median wouldn't move nearly as much.
lessons.careerRelevance: Data and ML teams use these statistics during data quality checks, experiment analysis, feature inspection, anomaly investigation, and model monitoring. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Exploratory data analysis (EDA)
objectives: Conduct a structured EDA pass on an unfamiliar dataset
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: time-series trend and seasonality.
Explain how EDA workflow changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect EDA workflow with distributions and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: EDA is the systematic first look at a new dataset before you draw any conclusions: check shape and types, look at distributions of each important column, check for correlations, and look for anything surprising.
examples:
df.shape, df.dtypes, df.describe()
df['category'].value_counts()
df.corr(numeric_only=True)   # look for surprising correlations
# then: histograms, scatter plots of the columns that matter most
commonMistakes: Skipping straight to modeling on a dataset you haven't explored — you'll often build a model on a column that's mostly nulls, or miss that two 'independent' features are actually.
lessons.careerRelevance: EDA is explicitly called out as its own competency in most data science and ML interview loops. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Data visualization & communicating insights
objectives: Pick an appropriate chart type and present a finding clearly
Explain how chart selection changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect chart selection with audience-first communication and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A chart's job is to make a pattern obvious at a glance — the wrong chart type (a pie chart for 15 categories, a line chart for unordered categories) obscures instead of clarifying. Communicating insights well means leading with the answer to the actual question being asked, not a dump of every chart you made along the way.
examples:
# Comparing categories -> bar chart, not pie (easier to compare bar heights than wedge angles)
# Trend over time -> line chart
# Relationship between 2 numeric vars -> scatter plot
commonMistakes: Showing a stakeholder ten exploratory charts instead of the one that answers their actual question — good communication is editing, not just plotting everything you looked at.
lessons.careerRelevance: The ability to explain a finding to a non-technical stakeholder is frequently the actual bar in data science interviews, not the code.

lessons.title: Feature preparation & reproducible analysis
objectives: Prepare features for modeling and make an analysis rerunnable
Explain how feature encoding changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect feature encoding with scaling and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Feature preparation means shaping cleaned data into the numeric, model-ready form an ML algorithm needs: encoding categories as numbers, scaling numeric ranges, and extracting useful derived columns (e.g. day-of-week from a date).
examples:
# reproducible: a script, not manual clicking
np.random.seed(42)
df['day_of_week'] = df['date'].dt.day_name()
df_encoded = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=['category'])
commonMistakes: Cleaning data manually in a spreadsheet with no record of the steps taken — nobody (including you, in 3 months) can reproduce or audit what was done.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is exactly the bridge into the Machine Learning track's 'feature engineering' topic.

lessons.title: Ethics, bias, and privacy
objectives: Identify common sources of bias and privacy risk in a dataset
Explain how sampling bias changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect sampling bias with proxy variables and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Data reflects the biases of how it was collected — a hiring dataset built from a company's past (biased) hiring decisions will encode that bias into any model trained on it.
examples:
# a classic bias trap:
# training a resume-screening model on 10 years of past hires
# --> it learns to reproduce whatever bias was in those past decisions,
#     even if the protected attribute itself was removed from the data
commonMistakes: Assuming removing a protected attribute (like gender) 'fixes' bias — other correlated columns (like name or zip code) can act as a proxy and reintroduce the same bias.
lessons.careerRelevance: Bias and privacy questions are now a standard, explicit part of ML/AI interview loops, not a specialist afterthought.

lessons.title: Model-ready data preprocessing pipelines
objectives: Build preprocessing that is fit on training data and reused consistently for validation and inference
Explain how scaling changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect scaling with encoding and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Model preprocessing converts raw data into stable features: missing-value handling, categorical encoding, numeric scaling, and text/image preparation. Any step that learns statistics must be fit only on training data, then reused unchanged on validation/test and production inputs.
lessons.example: Workflow: split train/validation first -> fit imputer/encoder/scaler on train -> transform train and validation -> save the fitted preprocessing objects with the model -> apply the same transformations during inference.
commonMistakes: Fitting preprocessing on the full dataset before the train/validation split.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in modern software/backend internship requirements or technical interviews and strengthens transferable engineering fundamentals.
